fixes.explanation: That's the word, baker. On hearing it, many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” That's a lot like me staring at a new recipe and announcing, "Who can accept this much dough?"

Not quite, friend. On hearing it, many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” They call it difficult, not familiar. In their own words, it's a hard teaching to accept.
I love a good compliment, but that's not what they say. The text has them saying, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” They call it difficult, and they ask who can accept it.
I see why you'd think so, but the text says Jesus was “Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching…” So He knew. That makes the statement false. Their grumbling didn't get past Him.
That's right. John 6:61 says Jesus was “Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching…” They're grumbling, and He knows it. Then He asks them, “Does this offend you?”
Good guess for a holy place, but the temple isn't in this sentence at all. Jesus says, “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” He names the Spirit as the One who gives life.

Yes, and the writer adds it right into the story: “For Jesus had known from the beginning which of them did not believe and who would betray Him.” So when Jesus says some of them don't believe, He isn't finding out right then. He already knew.

That would be a nice ending, and honestly I'd have loved it. But the text says, “From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.” They turned back, and I think that's a sad turn in the story.

Arguing isn't mentioned here. The text says, “…many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.” They stopped walking with Him, and that's all we're told. No synagogue and no arguing are in that verse.
You got it. Jesus turns to the Twelve and asks, “Do you want to leave too?” Many disciples have just turned back (John 6:66), and now He puts the question straight to the Twelve.
I see why a bigger group comes to mind, but the text says, “So Jesus asked the Twelve…” He asks the Twelve. That's who the question goes to.
The Pharisees aren't named anywhere in this passage. John 6:67 says, “So Jesus asked the Twelve…” So the question goes to the Twelve. I'd have asked the folks closest to me too.

That's a kind thing to point to, but it isn't what Peter says. Simon Peter, one of the Twelve, says, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.” That's his whole reason, and it's all about what Jesus says.
Right on. Peter says, “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” He says it straight to Jesus. And notice he says both believe and know.
Peter doesn't compare Jesus to anybody here. What he says is, “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” He says it plain.
Peter isn't describing a teacher at all. He says something much bigger: “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” He's saying who Jesus is.
Not quite, friend. That isn't the word the writer uses. John 6:71 says, “…he was later to betray Jesus.” Betray is the word for Judas here. I'd keep that one in your pocket.
